cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside compost collection program so food scraps are diverted from landfills.
2. Partner with grocery stores to donate unsold but safe food to local food banks and shelters.
3. Create a city-sponsored mobile app that alerts residents to discounted surplus food at nearby restaurants and markets.
4. Offer tax incentives to businesses that track and reduce their food waste.
5. Install community refrigerators in public spaces where people can leave and take surplus food.
6. Require large food businesses to separate organic waste from general trash.
7. Fund a "gleaning" program where volunteers harvest leftover crops from regional farms.
8. Run a public awareness campaign explaining the difference between "best by," "sell by," and "use by" labels.
9. Introduce pay-as-you-throw trash pricing to encourage households to waste less.
10. Establish a food rescue logistics hub with refrigerated vans to transport donations quickly.
11. Teach food waste reduction and meal planning in public school curricula.
12. Implement "offer versus serve" policies in school cafeterias so students take only what they will eat.
13. Schedule recess before lunch in elementary schools, which has been shown to reduce plate waste.
14. Host free community cooking classes focused on using leftovers and food scraps.
15. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion options at lower prices.
16. Provide free compostable takeout containers to restaurants that promote taking leftovers home.
17. Build an anaerobic digester at the wastewater plant to turn food waste into energy.
18. Distribute free countertop compost bins and kitchen caddies to residents.
19. Support "ugly produce" sections in grocery stores with promotional signage and city recognition.
20. Create a certification program that publicly recognizes "Zero Waste" restaurants and caterers.
21. Partner with local breweries and bakeries to repurpose spent grain and stale bread into new products.
22. Connect food businesses with farms that can use food scraps as animal feed where regulations allow.
23. Establish neighborhood community gardens that accept and use local compost.
24. Publicize state and federal Good Samaritan laws that protect food donors from liability.
25. Fund a food waste audit program that helps businesses measure exactly what they throw away.
26. Offer municipal grants for startups that upcycle food waste into sellable goods.
27. Require city-run events and festivals to include food donation and composting plans.
28. Train hospital and university dining staff in waste-reducing inventory and prep practices.
29. Run a "Shop Your Fridge First" social media challenge to encourage residents to cook what they have.
30. Create a public dashboard tracking the city's food waste diversion progress.
31. Coordinate with farmers markets to collect unsold produce at the end of each market day.
32. Set up drop-off compost sites at libraries, parks, and community centers for apartment dwellers.
33. Encourage grocery stores to use dynamic pricing that automatically discounts food nearing its expiration date.
34. Support volunteer-run "repair cafés" for food, where people learn preserving, canning, and fermenting.
35. Partner with senior centers to share bulk-purchased food and reduce spoilage for single-person households.
36. Lend food dehydrators and canning equipment through the public library system.
37. Require city procurement contracts for food services to include waste-reduction targets.
38. Develop a restaurant "doggy bag" campaign to normalize taking leftovers home.
39. Incentivize grocery stores to sell loose produce so shoppers can buy exactly the quantity they need.
40. Organize community potlucks or "disco soups" that turn rescued food into free public meals.
41. Pilot smart bins in commercial kitchens that weigh and log discarded food.
42. Create a regional food surplus marketplace connecting wholesalers with nonprofits and processors.
43. Offer free fridge thermometers and storage guides to help residents keep food fresh longer.
44. Fund culinary job-training programs that cook with rescued food, building both skills and meals.
45. Work with apartment managers to add organics collection to multifamily buildings.
46. Encourage corporate cafeterias to switch from buffet service to made-to-order meals.
47. Ban commercial food waste from landfills once sufficient composting capacity is in place.
48. Provide compost produced from city programs back to residents and urban farms for free.
49. Partner with local universities to research and evaluate the city's food waste interventions.
50. Appoint a dedicated food systems coordinator in city government to oversee all waste-reduction efforts.

cells.text:
## Households
1. Distribute free fridge thermometers and storage guides so residents keep produce at temperatures that extend its life.
2. Run a city-sponsored meal-planning app that builds shopping lists from what residents already have at home.
3. Launch a "use-it-up" recipe campaign on transit ads featuring dishes made from common leftovers like stale bread and wilting greens.
4. Offer workshops at libraries on pickling, fermenting, and freezing surplus food.
5. Mail every household a magnetic "eat first" bin label for the fridge to flag items nearing their end.
6. Create neighborhood sharing fridges where residents can drop off and pick up unopened or homemade surplus food.
7. Partner with utilities to include personalized food-waste tips and estimated dollar losses on monthly bills.

## Restaurants
8. Subsidize kitchen waste-tracking scales that log discarded food by category so chefs can adjust prep quantities.
9. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion options at reduced prices.
10. Give a city "Zero Waste Kitchen" certification that restaurants can display and market to diners.
11. Normalize takeaway by providing participating restaurants with branded reusable leftover containers.
12. Connect restaurants to apps that sell end-of-day surplus meals at a discount.
13. Host chef-led trainings on whole-ingredient cooking, such as using vegetable trimmings for stocks and sauces.
14. Encourage buffets and catering services to switch to smaller serving trays that are refilled more often.

## Grocers
15. Require or incentivize grocers to standardize date labels to "best by" and "use by" so shoppers stop discarding safe food.
16. Promote dedicated "imperfect produce" sections that sell cosmetically flawed fruits and vegetables at lower prices.
17. Support dynamic pricing technology that automatically discounts items as they approach their sell-by date.
18. Set up standing pickup agreements between every supermarket and local food banks for daily surplus donations.
19. Fund upgrades to energy-efficient refrigerated display cases that reduce spoilage.
20. Encourage stores to sell loose produce so customers buy only the quantity they need.
21. Partner with grocers to turn near-expiry produce into in-store prepared foods like soups and smoothies.

## Schools
22. Schedule recess before lunch, which studies show reduces plate waste because students arrive hungrier and less rushed.
23. Install share tables in cafeterias where students can leave unopened items for classmates to take.
24. Run student-led waste audits that weigh cafeteria discards and report results to the school community.
25. Let students choose their own sides under "offer versus serve" rules instead of receiving fixed trays.
26. Build school gardens that link food growing to lessons about the value of food.
27. Extend lunch periods to at least 20 minutes of seated eating time so children can finish their meals.
28. Send unserved cafeteria food to after-school programs and weekend backpack meal initiatives.

## Farms and Markets
29. Organize volunteer gleaning crews that harvest crops left in fields after commercial picking.
30. Create a regional online marketplace where farmers can list surplus or seconds for restaurants and processors.
31. Provide shared cold-storage facilities at farmers markets so unsold produce can be kept for the next day.
32. Fund a community processing kitchen where farmers can turn surplus into sauces, jams, and frozen goods.
33. Encourage market vendors to offer end-of-day bulk "rescue boxes" at reduced prices.
34. Offer tax credits to farmers who donate edible surplus to food banks.
35. Connect farms with livestock producers to redirect unsellable crops into animal feed.

## Municipal Policy
36. Phase in a ban on sending commercial food waste to landfill, starting with the largest generators.
37. Adopt pay-as-you-throw trash pricing so households pay less when they waste less.
38. Publicize liability protections for food donors so businesses no longer fear donating surplus.
39. Write food-waste reduction requirements into city procurement contracts for events, jails, and public cafeterias.
40. Appoint a city food-waste coordinator responsible for meeting a measurable reduction target.
41. Publish an annual public dashboard tracking the city's food waste by sector.
42. Offer small grants to startups and nonprofits developing food rescue or upcycling ventures.
43. Require large venues and event permits to include a food donation and composting plan.

## Composting and Recovery
44. Roll out curbside organics collection bins to every residential address.
45. Install community compost drop-off sites at parks, libraries, and transit hubs.
46. Distribute discounted backyard composters and worm bins to residents with yard space.
47. Partner with a wastewater treatment plant or anaerobic digester to convert unavoidable food scraps into biogas.
48. Give finished city compost back to residents and community gardens for free.
49. Support a food rescue dispatch app that coordinates volunteer drivers to move surplus from donors to shelters.
50. Help local breweries and bakeries send spent grain and stale bread to upcyclers that turn them into flour, snacks, or beer.

cells.state_text: A grandmother turning Tuesday's stale bread into Thursday's pudding, and a city bus map with its fixed loops. They meet in second chances that run on schedule. Maybe most waste isn't carelessness but bad timing: surplus appears where no route passes. A mid-size city might already have the loops it needs, delivery vans, school runs, transit, if leftovers could ride them the way bread rode the week toward pudding.
cells.text:
1. Equip city buses on their final evening loops with insulated lockers, so bakeries and cafés along the route can drop unsold food for pickup at end-of-line community hubs.
2. Partner with parcel delivery companies so their vans carry surplus groceries on the empty return leg of their daily routes back to the depot.
3. Use school buses on their midday deadhead runs to move surplus from school cafeterias to senior centers.
4. Publish a citywide "surplus timetable" showing when and where restaurants, grocers, and caterers reliably have leftovers, so charities can plan collections around the schedule instead of chasing random calls.
5. Have garbage trucks carry a separate sealed bin for edible surplus that gets diverted to a food bank before the landfill stop.
6. Equip ride-share and taxi drivers with an app that pays them a small fee to carry a surplus box when a donor and recipient lie along a trip they're already taking.
7. Place refrigerated community fridges at transit transfer stations, where foot traffic is high and restocking can follow bus schedules.
8. Give a fixed weekly "second-day" slot to every farmers' market, when unsold produce is sold at deep discount or handed to pre-registered pantries.
9. Have postal carriers collect sealed, nonperishable food donations from mailboxes on designated days, as some national food drives already do, but monthly instead of yearly.
10. Run a municipal "leftover lunch" program that turns hospital and corporate cafeteria surplus into packaged meals for shelters the same afternoon.
11. Build a shared commercial kitchen where volunteers and culinary students cook rescued ingredients into soups, sauces, and puddings that keep longer.
12. Offer grocery stores a tax credit for dynamic pricing that automatically marks down items as they approach expiration.
13. Standardize date labels across the city's retailers to a clear "best before" versus "use by" distinction, reducing confusion-driven discards.
14. Launch a neighborhood "bread to pudding" recipe campaign that teaches households to turn common leftovers into planned second meals later in the week.
15. Install smart compost bins in apartment complexes that weigh discarded food and send residents monthly waste feedback.
16. Create a city-run surplus-matching app where restaurants post leftovers and nearby shelters claim them within a set pickup window.
17. Have breweries and juice bars send spent grain and pulp to local bakers and farmers on a fixed weekly collection run.
18. Require large supermarkets to donate edible unsold food rather than discard it, following France's model.
19. Fund a "gleaning corps" that harvests unpicked crops from farms on the city's edge and delivers them via existing wholesale truck routes.
20. Sell "ugly produce" boxes through school fundraisers, giving cosmetically imperfect food a guaranteed buyer.
21. Add food rescue pickups to the routes of existing Meals on Wheels drivers, who already travel between kitchens and homes daily.
22. Offer residents discounted transit passes in exchange for volunteering as food runners on their regular commutes.
23. Shift restaurant portion sizes by offering "small plate" options, with a city sticker program recognizing participating venues.
24. Convert food that can't be eaten into animal feed by partnering with local farms on scheduled pickup routes.
25. Build an anaerobic digester at the wastewater plant that turns food scraps into biogas to power city vehicles.
26. Teach food-preservation classes on pickling, freezing, fermenting, and drying at public libraries.
27. Put community freezers in libraries and recreation centers so surplus perishables can be frozen before they spoil.
28. Coordinate school cafeteria "share tables" where students leave untouched packaged items for classmates or for after-school programs.
29. Time municipal compost collection to the day after weekends and holidays, when household food waste peaks.
30. Give caterers and event venues a default contract clause directing all leftover food to a pre-arranged rescue partner.
31. Use idle food truck capacity on slow weekdays to serve meals cooked from rescued ingredients at pay-what-you-can prices.
32. Create a "surplus bakery hour" in which participating bakeries sell the day's remaining bread at closing for a flat low price.
33. Install shelf sensors in grocery stores that flag aging produce to staff in time for markdowns or donations.
34. Set up a corporate pledge program in which office buildings commit to measuring and halving their cafeteria waste.
35. Fund university research on the city's specific waste hotspots, mapping where surplus appears with no rescue route nearby.
36. Redraw food-bank collection routes based on that surplus map so trucks pass the biggest sources at the right times.
37. Offer microgrants for neighborhood soup nights that cook whatever surplus the week has produced.
38. Pair restaurants with nearby homeless shelters in "kitchen sister" relationships with standing nightly pickups.
39. Launch a public awareness campaign on buses and bus shelters showing the average household's weekly waste cost.
40. Encourage households to keep a fridge "eat first" bin for items nearing expiration, promoted through utility bill inserts.
41. Provide liability protection education so businesses understand they're legally shielded when donating food in good faith.
42. Have hotels donate unopened breakfast buffet items to morning shelter programs via a standing daily courier.
43. Create a citywide reusable container system for transporting rescued food, so the logistics don't generate new waste.
44. Offer a "surplus subscription" in which residents pay weekly for a mystery box of rescued food collected along delivery routes.
45. Train cooks at institutional kitchens like jails, hospitals, and universities in nose-to-tail and root-to-stem cooking.
46. Hold an annual city competition awarding the business that rescues the most food per square foot.
47. Charge commercial waste haulers lower tipping fees for loads with food separated out for compost or digestion.
48. Partner with pet food producers to process safe but unsellable meat and fish trimmings.
49. Set up drop-off lockers at schools where parents leave surplus garden produce for families to take at pickup time.
50. Appoint a city "food flow coordinator" whose job is to align surplus timing with the routes, kitchens, and people who can use it.

1. Local farmers sell cosmetically imperfect produce at a discounted "seconds" stall that the city sets up at its farmers markets.
2. Volunteer gleaning crews harvest crops left in fields after commercial picking and deliver them to food pantries.
3. A regional food hub contracts with nearby farms to buy surplus at harvest peaks and freeze, can, or dry it for year-round sale.
4. Wholesale distributors link their ordering software to retailers' real-time sales data so they stop overshipping perishables.
5. Small producers share refrigerated trucks and cold storage through a city-subsidized cooperative so produce doesn't spoil in transit.
6. Local food processors turn off-spec vegetables and fruit into soups, sauces, and jams sold in area stores.

**Grocers**
7. Grocery stores use electronic shelf labels that automatically mark down items as they approach their date labels.
8. Supermarkets sell bruised or misshapen produce in low-cost "rescue bags" near the checkout.
9. Grocers replace confusing "sell by" stamps on store-packaged goods with a standard "best if used by" label.
10. Stores offer loose produce and smaller pack sizes so single-person households buy only what they'll eat.
11. Grocery delis turn day-old produce and meat into prepared salads, soups, and hot meals.
12. Store managers schedule nightly pickups so food banks collect unsold bread and baked goods.
13. Grocery chains run weekly shrink audits by department and adjust orders based on what gets thrown out.

**Restaurants**
14. Restaurants add half-portion and small-plate options to their menus.
15. Commercial kitchens weigh discarded trimmings and spoiled food with tracking scales to find where waste starts.
16. Chefs design menus that use the same ingredients across several dishes so fewer items expire unused.
17. Restaurants list end-of-day surplus meals at a discount on apps like Too Good To Go.
18. Caterers sign standing agreements with shelters to donate untouched event food within hours.
19. Servers offer compostable containers for leftovers by default rather than waiting for diners to ask.
20. Buffet operators switch to smaller plates and cook-to-order stations to cut tray waste.

**Households**
21. The city runs a public "Save the Food" campaign with bus ads and social posts showing how to store common foods.
22. Public libraries lend canning kits, dehydrators, and vacuum sealers along with how-to guides.
23. Community centers host free classes on cooking with leftovers and using vegetable scraps.
24. The utility department mails a fridge storage guide and a free fridge thermometer with water bills.
25. Neighborhood groups set up and maintain community fridges where residents can leave and take extra food.
26. The city partners with a meal-planning app to give residents free premium access that builds shopping lists from what they already have.
27. Households sign up for a four-week food waste challenge that provides a measuring caddy and tracks their progress.

**Schools and Institutions**
28. School districts schedule recess before lunch so students come in hungry and eat more of their meals.
29. Cafeterias set up share tables where students leave unopened milk, fruit, and packaged items for others.
30. Hospitals switch patients to on-demand room-service meals instead of preset trays.
31. University dining halls go trayless so students take only what they can carry and eat.
32. School boards lengthen lunch periods to at least 20 minutes of seated eating time.
33. Corporate cafeterias, jails, and senior centers run quarterly plate-waste audits and adjust portions and menus.

**Redistribution**
34. The city funds refrigerated vans so food banks can collect perishable donations safely.
35. A city-backed online platform matches businesses that have surplus food with nearby pantries in real time.
36. The regional food bank runs a commercial kitchen that turns donated surplus into frozen ready-to-eat meals.
37. The health department publishes plain-language guidance on Good Samaritan liability protections to reassure hesitant donors.
38. Volunteer bike couriers pick up small donations from cafés and corner stores that are too small for truck routes.
39. Food pantries accept past-"best by" shelf-stable goods using a posted safe-to-eat timeline.

**Composting and Recovery**
40. The sanitation department adds weekly curbside organics collection alongside trash and recycling.
41. Apartment complexes install shared, rodent-proof compost bins with city-provided collection.
42. The wastewater treatment plant co-digests food scraps in anaerobic digesters to make biogas.
43. Breweries and bakeries send spent grain and stale bread to local livestock farms as animal feed where regulations allow.
44. Community gardens run staffed drop-off compost sites on weekends.
45. The city gives finished compost free to residents, schools, and park crews to close the loop.

46. City council passes an ordinance requiring large food businesses to donate edible surplus and compost the rest.
47. The city adopts pay-as-you-throw trash pricing so households pay less when they divert food scraps.
48. The economic development office offers small grants to businesses that buy waste-tracking or food-preservation equipment.
49. The waste department runs an annual waste characterization study and publishes the results on a public dashboard.
50. City procurement rules require food-service contractors at city facilities to measure and report their food waste.

I'll sort the ideas by tone (comedy, dread, tenderness, absurd) and keep them distinct before numbering.

cells.state_text: Hitchcock's *Rope*, one apartment, a body in the chest, and Perec writing a whole novel without the letter *e*. Both treat the missing thing as the plot: the lid nobody opens, the vowel nobody says. Maybe the room is never just a set but the third actor, and each two-minute film is born from subtracting something (a door, a word, a light, the truth) and watching two people work around the hole.

1. A couple hosts a quiet dinner for two on top of a locked trunk, and the longer neither mentions what's inside, the more we suspect what it is.
2. Two siblings clear out their late mother's bedroom, each secretly searching for the same letter, and slowly realize the other already found it.
3. A job candidate faces an interviewer who never asks a single question, so she has to interview herself out loud until she admits why she wants to leave her old life.
4. During a blackout, two roommates confess things they'd never say in the light, then the power snaps back and neither can look up.
5. A woman asks her husband to help her rehearse a speech for leaving her husband, and he earnestly gives her notes.
6. A couple who made a pact never to say "no" to each other negotiate a pregnancy test result using every other word in the language.
7. Two people speak a full argument without ever using the letter *e*, and the strain of the missing vowel becomes the strain of the missing apology.
8. A painter and her model spend the session debating the portrait, which faces away from us until the final frame reveals a blank canvas.
9. Two strangers sit in a clinic waiting room whose inner door never opens, and gradually work out that they're waiting for the same patient.
10. A father and teenage son who aren't speaking communicate only by fighting over the TV remote's volume and channel.
11. In a hospital room with no clock, a nurse and a dying man bargain over what time it is, because he's decided he'll go at midnight.
12. A dinner table is set for three, and two people eat around the empty chair until one finally pours wine into its glass.
13. Two roommates paint over their only window to sleep through the day, and the room shrinks as their friendship curdles.
14. A phone rings on the table between a couple for the entire film, and each refuses to answer because both know who it is.
15. Two safecrackers open a vault room's safe to find it empty and must decide which of them is lying.
16. A bride at her final fitting talks to her seamstress about everything except the groom, and the seamstress pins the dress tighter with every evasion.
17. An elderly couple plays chess with no pieces, from memory, and one of them is beginning to forget the board.
18. A therapist realizes her client is lying about everything and starts answering only the lies.
19. Two estranged friends meet to return a borrowed book, and neither mentions the handwritten dedication on the first page.
20. A woman wakes in a hotel room beside a man she doesn't remember, and he pretends not to remember her either, for a reason he can't admit.
21. A man records his voicemail greeting over and over while his partner critiques each take, until the last one becomes a goodbye.
22. Two actors rehearse a play whose final page is missing and improvise an ending that turns out to be about their real marriage.
23. A granddaughter teaches her grandfather to make video calls, and the only contact he wants to call has been dead for a year.
24. A landlord inspects an apartment while the tenant insists there is no cat, as an increasingly enormous amount of evidence suggests otherwise.
25. Two people sharing a bed in a cold room tug one blanket back and forth until the tug-of-war becomes the conversation they've avoided.
26. A sculptor chips away at a block of stone while her ex sits for her, and with each strike, more of the truth about their breakup falls away.
27. In a deposition room, a witness answers every question but refuses to say the defendant's name, because it's also her own last name.
28. A kidnapper and his hostage slowly trade roles as she proves she knows more about the ransom than he does.
29. A room is stripped of every sound but a dripping tap, and two people fall into a silent argument timed to the drip.
30. A mother teaches her son to tie a necktie for his father's funeral, the knot she tied for his father every morning for thirty years.
31. A couple assembles flat-pack furniture with one piece missing, and the wobbling bookshelf becomes a referendum on their relationship.
32. After closing, an escape-room employee refuses to let the last player out until he solves a puzzle she built about him.
33. In a confessional, a priest recognizes the voice on the other side of the screen as his brother's.
34. A couple counts down to New Year's with the TV broken, and they can't agree on when midnight is, or whether to kiss.
35. A pianist's page-turner deliberately skips a page during a rehearsal, forcing the pianist to play from memory the piece she wrote for him.
36. A wordless film in which two people communicate only by flicking the room's light switch on and off.
37. A package arrives addressed to both roommates, and the entire film is them deciding whether to open it.
38. A detective interrogates a suspect with no evidence at all, and the suspect knows it and keeps him talking anyway.
39. A daughter reads her parents' old love letters aloud to her father, and he realizes from the dates that they weren't written by him.
40. In a darkroom, two photographers watch a print develop, and the image slowly reveals what one of them did last weekend.
41. A son plays the role of his own father because his mother, who has dementia, believes it's 1987 and her husband just came home.
42. Two clowns remove their makeup after a children's party, and each layer wiped away uncovers how badly the day really went.
43. A couple who don't share a language try to break up without a translator, and the misunderstandings keep accidentally reconciling them.
44. A woman cuts her partner's hair in total silence, and the length of each cut tells us how angry she is.
45. Two movers carry out the last items from an emptied apartment, and when one realizes the other is the former tenant, they slow down.
46. Two people stuck inside during a storm play twenty questions, and the object one of them is thinking of is the secret she came to tell.
47. A man returns a ring to a pawnshop and the broker recognizes it as the one she pawned years ago.
48. A mirror is missing from a theater dressing room, so an aging actress asks her understudy to describe her face before the show.
49. A woman makes a cup of tea for her intruding burglar and talks him into sitting until the police she called never arrive.
50. Two people stand in a room that is slowly being emptied around them by unseen hands, and they argue over which of them should be the last thing to go.

cells.brief: List 50 distinct ideas for reducing food waste in a mid-size city. Number them 1 to 50. One sentence each.
cells.text:
1. Launch a citywide curbside compost collection program so food scraps are diverted from landfills.
2. Partner with grocery stores to donate unsold but safe food to local food banks and shelters.
3. Create a city-sponsored mobile app that alerts residents to discounted surplus food at nearby restaurants and markets.
4. Offer tax incentives to businesses that track and reduce their food waste.
5. Install community refrigerators in public spaces where people can leave and take surplus food.
6. Require large food businesses to separate organic waste from general trash.
7. Fund a "gleaning" program where volunteers harvest leftover crops from regional farms.
8. Run a public awareness campaign explaining the difference between "best by," "sell by," and "use by" labels.
9. Introduce pay-as-you-throw trash pricing to encourage households to waste less.
10. Establish a food rescue logistics hub with refrigerated vans to transport donations quickly.
11. Teach food waste reduction and meal planning in public school curricula.
12. Implement "offer versus serve" policies in school cafeterias so students take only what they will eat.
13. Schedule recess before lunch in elementary schools, which has been shown to reduce plate waste.
14. Host free community cooking classes focused on using leftovers and food scraps.

6. Create neighborhood sharing fridges where residents can drop off and pick up unopened or homemade surplus food.
7. Partner with utilities to include personalized food-waste tips and estimated dollar losses on monthly bills.

## Restaurants
8. Subsidize kitchen waste-tracking scales that log discarded food by category so chefs can adjust prep quantities.
9. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portion options at reduced prices.
10. Give a city "Zero Waste Kitchen" certification that restaurants can display and market to diners.
11. Normalize takeaway by providing participating restaurants with branded reusable leftover containers.
12. Connect restaurants to apps that sell end-of-day surplus meals at a discount.
13. Host chef-led trainings on whole-ingredient cooking, such as using vegetable trimmings for stocks and sauces.
14. Encourage buffets and catering services to switch to smaller serving trays that are refilled more often.

## Grocers

16. Promote dedicated "imperfect produce" sections that sell cosmetically flawed fruits and vegetables at lower prices.

18. Set up standing pickup agreements between every supermarket and local food banks for daily surplus donations.
19. Fund upgrades to energy-efficient refrigerated display cases that reduce spoilage.
20. Encourage stores to sell loose produce so customers buy only the quantity they need.

43. Require large venues and event permits to include a food donation and composting plan.

cells.state_text: A grandmother turning Tuesday's stale bread into Thursday's pudding, and a city bus map with its fixed loops. They meet in second chances that run on schedule. Maybe most waste isn't carelessness but bad timing: surplus appears where no route passes. A mid-size city might already have the loops it needs, delivery vans, school runs, transit, if leftovers could ride them the way bread rode the week toward pudding.
cells.text:
1. Equip city buses on their final evening loops with insulated lockers, so bakeries and cafés along the route can drop unsold food for pickup at end-of-line community hubs.
2. Partner with parcel delivery companies so their vans carry surplus groceries on the empty return leg of their daily routes back to the depot.
3. Use school buses on their midday deadhead runs to move surplus from school cafeterias to senior centers.
4. Publish a citywide "surplus timetable" showing when and where restaurants, grocers, and caterers reliably have leftovers, so charities can plan collections around the schedule instead of chasing random calls.
5. Have garbage trucks carry a separate sealed bin for edible surplus that gets diverted to a food bank before the landfill stop.
6. Equip ride-share and taxi drivers with an app that pays them a small fee to carry a surplus box when a donor and recipient lie along a trip they're already taking.
7. Place refrigerated community fridges at transit transfer stations, where foot traffic is high and restocking can follow bus schedules.
8. Give a fixed weekly "second-day" slot to every farmers' market, when unsold produce is sold at deep discount or handed to pre-registered pantries.
9. Have postal carriers collect sealed, nonperishable food donations from mailboxes on designated days, as some national food drives already do, but monthly instead of yearly.
10. Run a municipal "leftover lunch" program that turns hospital and corporate cafeteria surplus into packaged meals for shelters the same afternoon.
11. Build a shared commercial kitchen where volunteers and culinary students cook rescued ingredients into soups, sauces, and puddings that keep longer.
12. Offer grocery stores a tax credit for dynamic pricing that automatically marks down items as they approach expiration.
13. Standardize date labels across the city's retailers to a clear "best before" versus "use by" distinction, reducing confusion-driven discards.
14. Launch a neighborhood "bread to pudding" recipe campaign that teaches households to turn common leftovers into planned second meals later in the week.
15. Install smart compost bins in apartment complexes that weigh discarded food and send residents monthly waste feedback.
16. Create a city-run surplus-matching app where restaurants post leftovers and nearby shelters claim them within a set pickup window.
17. Have breweries and juice bars send spent grain and pulp to local bakers and farmers on a fixed weekly collection run.
18. Require large supermarkets to donate edible unsold food rather than discard it, following France's model.
19. Fund a "gleaning corps" that harvests unpicked crops from farms on the city's edge and delivers them via existing wholesale truck routes.
20. Sell "ugly produce" boxes through school fundraisers, giving cosmetically imperfect food a guaranteed buyer.
21. Add food rescue pickups to the routes of existing Meals on Wheels drivers, who already travel between kitchens and homes daily.
22. Offer residents discounted transit passes in exchange for volunteering as food runners on their regular commutes.
23. Shift restaurant portion sizes by offering "small plate" options, with a city sticker program recognizing participating venues.
24. Convert food that can't be eaten into animal feed by partnering with local farms on scheduled pickup routes.
25. Build an anaerobic digester at the wastewater plant that turns food scraps into biogas to power city vehicles.
26. Teach food-preservation classes on pickling, freezing, fermenting, and drying at public libraries.
27. Put community freezers in libraries and recreation centers so surplus perishables can be frozen before they spoil.
28. Coordinate school cafeteria "share tables" where students leave untouched packaged items for classmates or for after-school programs.
29. Time municipal compost collection to the day after weekends and holidays, when household food waste peaks.
30. Give caterers and event venues a default contract clause directing all leftover food to a pre-arranged rescue partner.
31. Use idle food truck capacity on slow weekdays to serve meals cooked from rescued ingredients at pay-what-you-can prices.
32. Create a "surplus bakery hour" in which participating bakeries sell the day's remaining bread at closing for a flat low price.
33. Install shelf sensors in grocery stores that flag aging produce to staff in time for markdowns or donations.
34. Set up a corporate pledge program in which office buildings commit to measuring and halving their cafeteria waste.
35. Fund university research on the city's specific waste hotspots, mapping where surplus appears with no rescue route nearby.
36. Redraw food-bank collection routes based on that surplus map so trucks pass the biggest sources at the right times.
37. Offer microgrants for neighborhood soup nights that cook whatever surplus the week has produced.
38. Pair restaurants with nearby homeless shelters in "kitchen sister" relationships with standing nightly pickups.
39. Launch a public awareness campaign on buses and bus shelters showing the average household's weekly waste cost.
40. Encourage households to keep a fridge "eat first" bin for items nearing expiration, promoted through utility bill inserts.
41. Provide liability protection education so businesses understand they're legally shielded when donating food in good faith.
42. Have hotels donate unopened breakfast buffet items to morning shelter programs via a standing daily courier.
43. Create a citywide reusable container system for transporting rescued food, so the logistics don't generate new waste.
44. Offer a "surplus subscription" in which residents pay weekly for a mystery box of rescued food collected along delivery routes.
45. Train cooks at institutional kitchens like jails, hospitals, and universities in nose-to-tail and root-to-stem cooking.
46. Hold an annual city competition awarding the business that rescues the most food per square foot.
47. Charge commercial waste haulers lower tipping fees for loads with food separated out for compost or digestion.
48. Partner with pet food producers to process safe but unsellable meat and fish trimmings.
49. Set up drop-off lockers at schools where parents leave surplus garden produce for families to take at pickup time.
50. Appoint a city "food flow coordinator" whose job is to align surplus timing with the routes, kitchens, and people who can use it.

5. Small producers share refrigerated trucks and cold storage through a city-subsidized cooperative so produce doesn't spoil in transit.
6. Local food processors turn off-spec vegetables and fruit into soups, sauces, and jams sold in area stores.

**Grocers**
7. Grocery stores use electronic shelf labels that automatically mark down items as they approach their date labels.
8. Supermarkets sell bruised or misshapen produce in low-cost "rescue bags" near the checkout.
9. Grocers replace confusing "sell by" stamps on store-packaged goods with a standard "best if used by" label.
10. Stores offer loose produce and smaller pack sizes so single-person households buy only what they'll eat.
11. Grocery delis turn day-old produce and meat into prepared salads, soups, and hot meals.
12. Store managers schedule nightly pickups so food banks collect unsold bread and baked goods.
13. Grocery chains run weekly shrink audits by department and adjust orders based on what gets thrown out.

18. Caterers sign standing agreements with shelters to donate untouched event food within hours.

cells.state_text: Walking out from the brief: one room, two actors, two minutes. The room is the engine, so each idea needs one object or rule that changes the room's meaning: a locked door, a ringing phone, a slow countdown. Two actors means one shift per film: a confession, a reversal, a misunderstanding. Nothing from the walk bears on it yet. I'll sort the ideas by tone (comedy, dread, tenderness, absurd) and keep them distinct before numbering.
cells.text:
**Comedy**

1. Two roommates argue over whose turn it is to kill a spider, until one admits he's been secretly feeding it for weeks.
2. A man rehearses a breakup speech on his girlfriend's houseplant, and she walks in halfway through to correct his grammar.
3. A couple assembling flat-pack furniture finds one extra screw, and the debate over where it belongs reveals who really wanted to move in together.
4. A job interviewer and a candidate realize mid-interview that they once dated, and both pretend not to know while the questions get increasingly pointed.
5. Two siblings cleaning out their late father's study find his will hidden in a crossword with the final clue left blank.
6. A first date at home derails when a smart speaker keeps answering questions nobody asked, using her search history.
7. A hostage negotiator practices on his wife in their kitchen and keeps caving to her demands.
8. Two strangers locked in an escape room realize the countdown clock has no batteries and nobody is watching.
9. A best man rehearses his toast for the groom, who slowly realizes every anecdote is about the bride.
10. A woman returns a borrowed sweater to her neighbor, and the lining holds a love letter neither will admit to writing.
11. Two actors at a table read can't stop laughing at one line until one reveals it's something her mother actually said.
12. A couple plays a board game where the loser confesses a secret, and one of them deliberately loses every round.

**Dread**

13. A babysitter and the boy she's minding hear the parents come home, and the boy whispers that those aren't his parents.
14. A man wakes beside his wife, who insists the bedroom window wasn't there yesterday.
15. Two people waiting out a storm notice the knocking at the door matches one of their heartbeats.
16. A therapist's client describes a recurring dream of this exact office, down to the cup the therapist is holding.
17. A kitchen timer counts down, and neither person will say what happens when it reaches zero.
18. A couple's answering machine plays a message from one of them, recorded tomorrow.
19. During a power cut, a couple counts each other's footsteps and keeps getting one too many.
20. Two night guards watch a monitor showing their own room with only one of them in it.
21. Two hikers sheltering in a cabin find a guestbook whose last entry is their names, in their own handwriting.
22. A mother takes her son's temperature, and the thermometer reads a number no living person could have.

24. A woman asks her husband to describe their wedding, and he gets everything right except who he married.
25. Two people trapped in a sealed room hear a phone ringing, though there is no phone.

**Tenderness**

26. An elderly man teaches his granddaughter to dance in the kitchen, and halfway through she realizes he thinks she's her grandmother.
27. Two exes divide their record collection, and every album sparks a memory that makes them hand it back.
28. A father braids his daughter's hair for the first time on the morning after her mother leaves.

cells.state_text: Hitchcock's *Rope*, one apartment, a body in the chest, and Perec writing a whole novel without the letter *e*. Both treat the missing thing as the plot: the lid nobody opens, the vowel nobody says. Maybe the room is never just a set but the third actor, and each two-minute film is born from subtracting something (a door, a word, a light, the truth) and watching two people work around the hole.

1. A couple hosts a quiet dinner for two on top of a locked trunk, and the longer neither mentions what's inside, the more we suspect what it is.
2. Two siblings clear out their late mother's bedroom, each secretly searching for the same letter, and slowly realize the other already found it.
3. A job candidate faces an interviewer who never asks a single question, so she has to interview herself out loud until she admits why she wants to leave her old life.
4. During a blackout, two roommates confess things they'd never say in the light, then the power snaps back and neither can look up.
5. A woman asks her husband to help her rehearse a speech for leaving her husband, and he earnestly gives her notes.
6. A couple who made a pact never to say "no" to each other negotiate a pregnancy test result using every other word in the language.
7. Two people speak a full argument without ever using the letter *e*, and the strain of the missing vowel becomes the strain of the missing apology.
8. A painter and her model spend the session debating the portrait, which faces away from us until the final frame reveals a blank canvas.
9. Two strangers sit in a clinic waiting room whose inner door never opens, and gradually work out that they're waiting for the same patient.
10. A father and teenage son who aren't speaking communicate only by fighting over the TV remote's volume and channel.
11. In a hospital room with no clock, a nurse and a dying man bargain over what time it is, because he's decided he'll go at midnight.
12. A dinner table is set for three, and two people eat around the empty chair until one finally pours wine into its glass.
13. Two roommates paint over their only window to sleep through the day, and the room shrinks as their friendship curdles.
14. A phone rings on the table between a couple for the entire film, and each refuses to answer because both know who it is.
15. Two safecrackers open a vault room's safe to find it empty and must decide which of them is lying.
16. A bride at her final fitting talks to her seamstress about everything except the groom, and the seamstress pins the dress tighter with every evasion.
17. An elderly couple plays chess with no pieces, from memory, and one of them is beginning to forget the board.
18. A therapist realizes her client is lying about everything and starts answering only the lies.
19. Two estranged friends meet to return a borrowed book, and neither mentions the handwritten dedication on the first page.
20. A woman wakes in a hotel room beside a man she doesn't remember, and he pretends not to remember her either, for a reason he can't admit.
21. A man records his voicemail greeting over and over while his partner critiques each take, until the last one becomes a goodbye.
22. Two actors rehearse a play whose final page is missing and improvise an ending that turns out to be about their real marriage.
23. A granddaughter teaches her grandfather to make video calls, and the only contact he wants to call has been dead for a year.
24. A landlord inspects an apartment while the tenant insists there is no cat, as an increasingly enormous amount of evidence suggests otherwise.
25. Two people sharing a bed in a cold room tug one blanket back and forth until the tug-of-war becomes the conversation they've avoided.
26. A sculptor chips away at a block of stone while her ex sits for her, and with each strike, more of the truth about their breakup falls away.
27. In a deposition room, a witness answers every question but refuses to say the defendant's name, because it's also her own last name.
28. A kidnapper and his hostage slowly trade roles as she proves she knows more about the ransom than he does.
29. A room is stripped of every sound but a dripping tap, and two people fall into a silent argument timed to the drip.
30. A mother teaches her son to tie a necktie for his father's funeral, the knot she tied for his father every morning for thirty years.
31. A couple assembles flat-pack furniture with one piece missing, and the wobbling bookshelf becomes a referendum on their relationship.
32. After closing, an escape-room employee refuses to let the last player out until he solves a puzzle she built about him.
33. In a confessional, a priest recognizes the voice on the other side of the screen as his brother's.
34. A couple counts down to New Year's with the TV broken, and they can't agree on when midnight is, or whether to kiss.
35. A pianist's page-turner deliberately skips a page during a rehearsal, forcing the pianist to play from memory the piece she wrote for him.
36. A wordless film in which two people communicate only by flicking the room's light switch on and off.
37. A package arrives addressed to both roommates, and the entire film is them deciding whether to open it.
38. A detective interrogates a suspect with no evidence at all, and the suspect knows it and keeps him talking anyway.
39. A daughter reads her parents' old love letters aloud to her father, and he realizes from the dates that they weren't written by him.
40. In a darkroom, two photographers watch a print develop, and the image slowly reveals what one of them did last weekend.
41. A son plays the role of his own father because his mother, who has dementia, believes it's 1987 and her husband just came home.
42. Two clowns remove their makeup after a children's party, and each layer wiped away uncovers how badly the day really went.
43. A couple who don't share a language try to break up without a translator, and the misunderstandings keep accidentally reconciling them.
44. A woman cuts her partner's hair in total silence, and the length of each cut tells us how angry she is.
45. Two movers carry out the last items from an emptied apartment, and when one realizes the other is the former tenant, they slow down.
46. Two people stuck inside during a storm play twenty questions, and the object one of them is thinking of is the secret she came to tell.
47. A man returns a ring to a pawnshop and the broker recognizes it as the one she pawned years ago.
48. A mirror is missing from a theater dressing room, so an aging actress asks her understudy to describe her face before the show.
49. A woman makes a cup of tea for her intruding burglar and talks him into sitting until the police she called never arrive.
50. Two people stand in a room that is slowly being emptied around them by unseen hands, and they argue over which of them should be the last thing to go.
